newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Officials assure S.Africans after Ebola death.
newsitem.headline: Officials assure S.Africans after Ebola death.

text.p: Health authorities assured South Africans on Monday that the deadly Ebola fever was under control after the death of a nurse who caught the disease from a Central African doctor.
Over 300 people were being monitored for signs of the fever, which originated in the jungles of Central Africa.
So far there was no sign that the disease was spreading, Gauteng provincial health spokesman Popo Maja said.

Marilyn Lahana, a 46-year-old mother of two who nursed a Gabonese doctor and contracted Ebola from him, died on Sunday night in a Johannesburg hospital isolation ward after suffering severe brain damage during a haemorrhage caused by the fever.
"We are satisfied that the disease is under control. Every technical measure has been taken to ensure that we contain (it)," Maja told Reuters.
Lahana was the first person inside South Africa to contract the disease, which causes extensive bleeding and degeneration of organs and arteries.
The doctor has returned home to Central Africa after Lahana treated him at the end of October for fever, later shown to have been brought on by Ebola.

The virus, which killed 245 people in Zaire last year and 35 people in two outbreaks in Gabon earlier this year, is fatal in 80 to 90 percent of cases. With early diagnosis the fatality rate can be lowered to around 30 percent.
Maja said officials were monitoring Lahana's relatives as well as hospital and laboratory staff who had worked on tissue samples taken from her and the Gabonese doctor.
Health authorities were eager to reassure people who were "unreasonably worried" about the fever, passed on through direct contact with bodily fluids of a carrier.
Maja said some children of hospital nurses had been turned away from classes near Johannesburg.
"It is an unfortunate development, but we have sent our counselling team to the school to reassure them that the nurses' children are under no risk."

World Health Organisation (WHO) doctor Brian Gushulak arrived in South Africa on Sunday to study the case and Maja said he had been "full of praise" for the authorities' handling of it, which could serve as a model for other countries.
